articles.text: County confirms cases of Omicron variant The Alameda County Public Health Department and the City of Berkeley released a joint statement on December 3 confirming five cases of the Omicron COVID variant in the county. The cases were identified by public health officials as “mildly symptomatic,” and are among 12 local COVID cases linked to a November 27 wedding in Wisconsin. One of the infected individuals attended the wedding upon return from international travel, the press release confirmed. A state-run lab used genomic sequencing to identify the five infected with the COVID-19 Omicron variant, which is now being detected around the world. Alameda County and the City of Berkeley Public Health Departments are investigating these cases with the assistance of the California Department of Public Health. All infected individuals and close contacts are being notified and provided with isolation and quarantine guidance; infected individuals range between the ages of 18 and 49. One is a resident of Berkeley, and the remaining twelve are Alameda County residents. All 12 individuals were vaccinated, and most had received booster shots. No one has been hospitalized as a result of their symptoms. “Public health officials continue to be vigilant and are monitoring evidence of this variant’s transmissibility and the severity of illness resulting from infection,” said ACPHD Public Information Officer Neetu Balram. “We don’t yet know how Omicron will impact a highly vaccinated region like the Bay Area. We remind residents that vaccination continues to provide the best protection against severe illness from COVID-19 that could result in hospitalization and death.” travel, whether international or domestic. State mask mandate reimposed As of today, December 15, the State of California will reimpose indoor mask mandates for all residents regardless of vaccination status in public settings. The mask requirement will be in place through January 15. The announcement was made by Health and Human Services Secretary Dr. Mark Ghaly on Monday, December 13. The news comes as Omicron variants have been detected throughout the state, with 18 cases reported statewide as of December 10. “This is a critical time. We have a tool we know has worked and can work,” Dr. Ghaly said. “We are proactively putting this tool of universal indoor masking in place [now] to ensure we get through a time of joy and hope without a darker cloud of despair. Californians have done this before, and we believe we can do it again.” In addition, the state will require those who attend “megaevents” of 1,000 or more people to show vaccination or proof of negative test taken within one day of arrival; the previous allowable window for testing before attending an event was 72 hours. The state is also recommending that travelers who return to California test three to five days after arrival. Dr. Ghaly confirmed that COVID case rates statewide have jumped 47% since the Thanksgiving holiday. Neetu Balram, Alameda County Public Health Dept. Both public health agencies are urging residents to continue to utilize known strategies that stop the spread of COVID. These include staying home if sick, washing hands diligently, wearing a mask indoors, and getting tested if symptomatic. articles.text: “Until the day dawns and the morning star rests in your hearts.” (II Peter 1:16-21) In the church of my youth much attention was paid to the second coming of Jesus. While no one, at least as far as I remember, was of the “I know the exact date it will occur so until then don’t count on me for anything” school of thought. Much attention was paid to world events, especially the establishment of the Nation of Israel in 1948, as clear signs that Jesus would soon physically return. Of course, we were not the first, or the last, to live with the expectation that the second coming was near at hand. Many, if not most, of the first followers of Jesus, expected that he would return while they were still alive. This belief made them courageous but it also meant that their ethics could be greatly influenced by a “it doesn’t matter because we are not long for this world” outlook. articles.text: For many a highlight of the holiday season is food. From turkey and mashed potatoes, to ham and stuffing, and latkes and challah, food can bring communities together and unify us with friends and family. However, the holiday season is often a time in which there is an excess of food wasted. According to CalRecycle’s waste characterization study in 2018, food waste comprised 13 percent of what we dispose annually. In fact, every year, Californians throw away 5-6 million tons of food waste. During the last edition of the Piedmont Post, the Climate Corner highlighted gifting ideas for “greening” the holidays across the three “R’s”: Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle. This week, the Piedmont Sustainability Team has compiled some tips and tricks to further green the holiday season by reducing food waste and a family’s carbon footprint. From purchasing to cooking, donating, and composting, there are significant ways to reduce the carbon footprint of your food both during and after the holiday season. Resources like the United Nations World Food Programme and #StopTheWaste campaign highlight how the food we purchase can significantly impact the carbon footprint. According to the UN, “food system” refers to the activities involved in producing, processing, transporting, and consuming food. Food systems touch every aspect of human existence. One aspect to consider is “food miles”, the distance travelled by your food before it reaches your plate, and the mode of transportation that transports your food. For instance, flying one ton of food is nearly 70 times more carbon intensive than transporting that same weight by rough other methods like a cargo ship. Shopping for food that has been produced and grown within a closer geographic region can reduce these food miles, and as a result, its carbon footprint. Consider supporting a nearby farmers market, where you can not only support local businesses, but have a conversation about where your food came from and how it was prepared. In addition to food miles, food preparation can impact your carbon footprint and your health. Did you know using a gas range stove releases pollutants into our homes and can produce unsafe levels of indoor air pollution? While most residential appliances vent pollution outside (think gas-powered furnaces and water heaters), your stove may be the one gas appliance that is likely unvented. Common pollutants from gas stoves include carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, and formaldehyde. Some ways to reduce these pollutants include opening windows, running exhaust fans and range hoods, using a HEPA air purifier with a carbon filter, and cooking using an electric induction cooktop rather than a gas range stove. Annie Wensley is the City of Piedmont’s Climate Action Fellow. She can be reached at awensley@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: “Greening” the Holidays: Food Edition

During the last edition of the Piedmont Post, the Climate Corner highlighted gifting ideas for “greening” the holidays across the three “R’s”: Reduce, Reuse, and Recycle. This week, the Piedmont Sustainability Team has compiled some tips and tricks to further green the holiday season by reducing food waste and a family’s carbon footprint. From purchasing to cooking, donating, and composting, there are significant ways to reduce the carbon footprint of your food both during and after the holiday season. Resources like the United Nations World Food Programme and #StopTheWaste campaign highlight how the food we purchase can significantly impact the carbon footprint. According to the UN, “food system” refers to the activities involved in producing, processing, transporting, and consuming food. Food systems touch every aspect of human existence. One aspect to consider is “food miles”, the distance travelled by your food before it reaches your plate, and the mode of transportation that transports your food. For instance, flying one ton of food is nearly 70 times more carbon intensive than transporting that same weight by rough other methods like a cargo ship. Shopping for food that has been produced and grown within a closer geographic region can reduce these food miles, and as a result, its carbon footprint. Consider supporting a nearby farmers market, where you can not only support local businesses, but have a conversation about where your food came from and how it was prepared. In addition to food miles, food preparation can impact your carbon footprint and your health. Did you know using a gas range stove releases pollutants into our homes and can produce unsafe levels of indoor air pollution? While most residential appliances vent pollution outside (think gas-powered furnaces and water heaters), your stove may be the one gas appliance that is likely unvented. Common pollutants from gas stoves include carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, and formaldehyde. Some ways to reduce these pollutants include opening windows, running exhaust fans and range hoods, using a HEPA air purifier with a carbon filter, and cooking using an electric induction cooktop rather than a gas range stove. articles.text: We get asked this question a lot by high school students: “When am I ever going to use Algebra or history in real life?” The short answer is that you probably won’t, but we need you to show that you can tackle high school before we want you building bridges or performing brain surgery. The long answer is that high school is about developing thinking skills, so when it comes time to do things as an adult, students are ready to use their mind to solve problems and achieve success. The Practicality of an Impractical Education In grammar school, we learned essential skills: reading, writing, and arithmetic. But it is harder to see the point of high school classes like Algebra, English Literature, Ancient History or Physics. So, if students are never going to actually use cosine, recite the causes of World War I, or write a 5-paragraph essay as an adult, what is the point? When my students ask why they have to learn what they are learning, I often ask them, “if your friends were accepted into medical school right now, do you think they would become very good doctors?” Generally, the answer is “no”. Most students recognize that they themselves and their peers are not really ready to tackle adult tasks. Their brains are not ready yet. Their ability to learn, think, comprehend, or problem-solve are not developed enough. That is why we teach what we teach in high school. We are working to develop these underlying cognitive skills that are required in our society. What are the “Skills” It’s possible to just memorize their way through school, but that will leave a student only able to follow instructions. What other skills can students develop in each class? Math and Science: To actually solve a problem (not just repeat memorized steps) someone must comprehend difficult concepts, solve logically, and use rigid, linear thinking. All of these cognitive abilities are essential to succeed in a business world in which we are forced to tackle problems for which there is no answer key or teacher’s notes. English and History: We disseminate information through the written word. When students are reading The Joy Luck Club or a history textbook, it is important that they develop the ability to thoroughly understand what they are reading. This skill is probably more important than the actual facts or themes in the reading. That’s not to say that learning history or understanding literature isn’t important – it is. But from a practical standpoint, it is more important that students learn to read for content than the content itself. The same goes for an essay. Is it really important that the world knows their opinion on the Industrial Revolution? Probably not, but one day every student will have a message they want to get out there, and when that happens, the ability to express oneself through the written word will be essential. Please send your suggestions to City Editor Allyson Aleksey at allysonaaleksey@gmail.com Thinking Outside The Classroom What do students get out of a high school education? By Paul Osborn We get asked this question a lot by high school students: “When am I ever going to use Algebra or history in real life?” The short answer is that you probably won’t, but we need you to show that you can tackle high school before we want you building bridges or performing brain surgery. The long answer is that high school is about developing thinking skills, so when it comes time to do things as an adult, students are ready to use their mind to solve problems and achieve success. The Practicality of an Impractical Education In grammar school, we learned essential skills: reading, writing, and arithmetic. But it is harder to see the point of high school classes like Algebra, English Literature, Ancient History or Physics. So, if students are never going to actually use cosine, recite the causes of World War I, or write a 5-paragraph essay as an adult, what is the point? When my students ask why they have to learn what they are learning, I often ask them, “if your friends were accepted into medical school right now, do you think they would become very good doctors?” Generally, the answer is “no”. Most students recognize that they themselves and their peers are not really ready to tackle adult tasks. Their brains are not ready yet. Their ability to learn, think, comprehend, or problem-solve are not developed enough. That is why we teach what we teach in high school. We are working to develop these underlying cognitive skills that are required in our society. What are the “Skills” It’s possible to just memorize their way through school, but that will leave a student only able to follow instructions. What other skills can students develop in each class? Math and Science: To actually solve a problem (not just repeat memorized steps) someone must comprehend difficult concepts, solve logically, and use rigid, linear thinking. All of these cognitive abilities are essential to succeed in a business world in which we are forced to tackle problems for which there is no answer key or teacher’s notes. English and History: We disseminate information through the written word. When students are reading The Joy Luck Club or a history textbook, it is important that they develop the ability to thoroughly understand what they are reading. This skill is probably more important than the actual facts or themes in the reading. That’s not to say that learning history or understanding literature isn’t important – it is. But from a practical standpoint, it is more important that students learn to read for content than the content itself. The same goes for an essay. Is it really important that the world knows their opinion on the Industrial Revolution? Probably not, but one day every student will have a message they want to get out there, and when that happens, the ability to express oneself through the written word will be essential. Next month we can go over ways to develop these skills in each class. Paul the Tutor (aka Paul Osborne) runs Paul the Tutor’s Education Services online and on Piedmont Avenue. articles.text: On a cold Christmas Eve in 1818, pastor Joseph Franz Mohr walked the three kilometers from his home in the Austrian village of Oberndorf bei Salzburg to visit his friend Franz Gruber in the neighboring town of Arnsdorf bei Laufen. Mohr brought with him a poem he had written two years earlier. He desperately needed a carol for his Christmas Eve midnight mass that evening. He hoped his friend Gruber, a school teacher who also served as the church’s choir master and organist, could set his poem to music. In a matter of a few hours, Franz Gruber composed the “Stille Nacht” melody for Mohr on that night of December 24, 1818. Flooding of the nearby Salzach River had put the church organ out of commission, so Gruber composed the music for guitar accompaniment. A few hours after Gruber finished the composition, he and Mohr stood before the altar at St. Nicholas Church in Oberndorf to perform the work. A local choir sang the new composition, breaking the silence of that “stille nacht.” Silent Night, Holy Night Mohr; English trans. by John Freeman Young. Silent, night, holy night, All is calm, all is bright. ’Round yon virgin, mother and child Holy infant so tender and mild, Sleep in heavenly peace, Sleep in heavenly peace. Silent night, holy night, Shepherds quake at the sight. Glories stream from heaven afar, Heavenly hosts sing Alleluia; Christ the Savior is born, Christ the Savior is born. Silent night, holy night, Son of God, love’s pure light. Radiant beams from Thy holy face, With the dawn of redeeming grace, Jesus, Lord at Thy birth; Jesus, Lord at Thy birth.
articles.title: Silent Night (Stille Nacht)

articles.text: The song “The 12 days of Christmas” has its origins as a teaching tool to instruct young people in the meaning and content of the Christian faith. articles.text: ’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care, In hopes that Saint Nicholas soon would be there. The children were nestled all snug in their beds, While visions of sugar plums danced in their heads; And mama in her kerchief, and I in my cap Had just settled our brains for a long winter’s nap. When out on the lawn there arose such a clatter I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, Tore open the shutter and threw open the sash. The moon on the breast of the new-fallen snow Gave a luster of midday to objects below; When to my wondering eyes should appear But a miniature sleigh and eight tiny reindeer. With a little old driver, so lively and quick, I knew in a moment it must be Saint Nick! More rapid than eagles his coursers they came, And he whistled and shouted and called them by name: “Now, Dasher! Now, Dancer! Now, Prancer! Now, Vixen! On, Comet! On, Cupid! On Donder and Blitzen! To the top of the porch, to the top of the wall, Now dash away, dash away, dash away all.” As dry leaves that before the wild hurricane fly, When they meet with an obstacle mount to the sky. So up to the housetop the coursers they flew, With a sleigh full of toys – and Saint Nicholas, too. And then in a twinkling, I heard on the roof The prancing and pawing of each little hoof. As I drew in my head and was turning around, Down the chimney Saint Nicholas came with a bound. He was dressed all in fur from his head to his foot, And his clothes were all tarnished with ashes and soot. A bundle of toys he had flung on his back, And he looked like a peddler just opening his pack. His eyes, how they twinkled! His dimples, how merry! His cheeks were like roses, his nose like a cherry! His droll little mouth was drawn up in a bow, And the beard on his chin was as white as the snow. The stump of a pipe he held tight in his teeth, And the smoke, it encircled his head like a wreath. He had a broad face and a little round belly That shook when he laughed like a bowl fully of jelly. He was chubby and plump, a right jolly old elf, And I laughed when I saw him in spite of myself. A wink of his eye and a twist of his head Soon gave me to know I had nothing to dread. He spoke not a word, but went straight to his work, And filled all the stockings; then turned with a jerk, And laying a finger aside of his nose, And giving a nod, up the chimney he rose. He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle, And away they all flew like the down of a thistle. But I heard him exclaim, ’ere they drove out of sight, “Happy Christmas to all, and to all a good night!” All services are available for streaming at the listed times or watching at one’s convenience 24/7 after the service has ended. articles.text: The Piedmont boys’ soccer team defeated San Lorenzo 4-1 on Friday, December 10 on the road. Two days earlier they sustained their first loss of the season, 3-2 against Mt. Eden in Hayward on December 8. Piedmont’s big win against San Lorenzo was a strong response to its loss to Mt. Eden, where the Monarchs pulled off a late upset with two goals in the final five minutes. “We played with a maturity that we haven’t showed a lot of,” said coach Todd Sullivan after the victory against San Lorenzo. “The loss came from a crazy position with five minutes to go, but we controlled the second half. That’s soccer. [The win] was a good reaction to what happened.” “We were in control against Mt. Eden. [Against San Lorenzo] we just wanted to take charge and put in a good performance. We have a [holiday] break and wanted to do well before that,” added senior Anders Payne, who scored his first goal in Friday’s game. San Lorenzo Recap The Highlanders’ first goal came in the 18th minute on a counter attack following a SLZ free kick. Senior captain Andre Stankiewicz whipped in a pass to Aiden Woolwine, who slotted in a hard shot to the keeper’s right. Piedmont went up 2-0 in the 32nd minute when Payne was able to walk one in. In the buildup, Stankiewicz drew a foul one yard above the penalty area to enable a free kick opportunity for Conner Curtis. His spot kick ricocheted off the cross bar and back toward Payne, whose initial header skipped off the cross bar, again, then back to his midsection for the tap in. “It was my first goal in four years,” he said. Luckily, Conner put in on target and I was just there,” said Payne. In the second half, Darius Grammer put PHS up 3-0 in the 49th minute. The play started when Patrick Alexander, appearing at right midfielder after being a center back, won the ball in SLZ’s defensive third and played it through to Woolwine on the Staff Photos Conner Curtis had a right-footed goal against San Lorenzo and a leftfooted score against Mt. Eden. Aiden Woolwine had a goal and had an assist in a 4-1 victory over San Lorenzo. right wing. Woolwine sent a cross all the way to Grammer on the left post, who took it off his chest then followed through for a leftfoot finish. articles.text: After a good (or, more accurately, bad) year’s COVID absence, the Chanticleer singers were back once more in exemplary form. We can properly celebrate Christmas again with their predictably profound and joyful sounds. The dozen male vocalists – the only ones in the entire hall without masks – won sustained ovations Sunday from the crowd at the Cathedral of Christ the Light in Oakland, as well as from Bishop Michael Barber in his low-key attendance as just one of many fans in the pews. We may not be back to normal yet, but no one will suppress the unbridled joy of the 2021 Christmas-holiday season. The usual elements of a cappella (unaccompanied) singing, multi-lingual repertoire and highrange countertenors were supplemented by innovations of the new music director, Tim Keeler. This meant linking of composers from vastly different centuries and backgrounds setting the same carol texts. So, the familiar carol “Lo, a Rose E’er Blooming” featured living composer Jonathan Woody as catalyst between Michael Praetorius and Hugo Distler, spanning four centuries in total. The more it’s the same, the more it’s different. This being the 400th anniversary of Praetorius’ passing, the emphasis was on German texts, as well as unharmonized Latin hymnody by the brilliant 12th century polymath German nun (and now saint), Hildegard von Bingen. The exhibition explores the values, strategies, and ways of life and culture in current feminist art. Artworks made in 2000 and beyond are the primary focus, but many installations on view span several generations, mediums, and geographies. The exhibition is organized around eight themes: hysteria; the gaze; revisiting historical subjects through a feminist lens; the fragmented female body; gender fluidity; labor, domesticity, and activism; female anger; and feminist utopias. New Time is inspired by Bay Area poet Leslie Scalapino’s feminist poem of the same name. Many female artists, groups, musicians, and activists are featured, including Judy Chicago, Laura Aguilar, Lynn Hershman Leeson, Nicole Eisenman, Kiki Smith, and Amy Sillman. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California has rescheduled the opening of Edith Heath: A Life in Clay to January 29, 2022. The exhibition was rescheduled due to water damage in the museum. The retrospect will be on display through October 30, 2022. A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video will be shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artists’ career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay was organized by Oakland Museum’s Curator of A sampling of ceramics by Edith Heath. Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than 50 years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Berkeley Symphony Nigel Armstrong (left), Emanuela Nikiforova, Ivo Bokulic, and Isaac Pastor-Chermak performed a stirring concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, December 12 The Berkeley Symphony does things right, and much of the credit must go to Artistic Director Rene Mandel. Their ongoing series of chamber music concerts, now in its ninth year at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, is a perfect example. All seemed calm on the surface in advance of Berkeley Symphony musicians’ opening chamber music concert of the 2021-22 season. And then I was informed of some heroic performances. A couple of the performers who were originally announced to play the concert had to cancel due to schedule conflicts. In ordinary times that might spell disaster, and usually the concert might be canceled. But it wasn’t. The substitute players played heroically. Winter from Antonio Vivaldi‘s ubiquitous Four Seasons served as a perfect warm up. That did not prepare the large and enthusiastic audience who had come on a cold and very wet Sunday afternoon for the surprise that awaited them. After the Vivaldi, guest violinist Nigel Armstrong strode to the stage and delivered Brian Nabors’ Theme and Variations for Solo Violin. His bow jumped over the strings like a graceful kangaroo, and there were other spectacular techniques as well. Armstrong made the difficult look like child’s play. His bow skipped along the string like a smooth stone skittering across the surface of a lake. That’s called a flying staccato. Not only that but Nabors’ composition calls for bowed notes to be combined with Pizzicato notes played simultaneously. Paganini invented this technique, but composer Brian Nabors gave it a 21st century touch. If it was difficult and virtuosic. What made it all the more interesting was that it was played with consummate ease. Immediately after the solo piece, Armstrong was joined by violinist Emanuella Nikiforova, violist Ivo Bokulic, and cellist Isaac Pastor-Chermak. They wowed the audience with a new piece, Jessie Montgomery’s string quartet entitled Voodoo Dolls. This was really scary stuff. It reminded me of the mythical labyrinth of Knossos. You know the story… a labyrinth is constructed to encage the minotaur, a beast of great ferocity. This ferocious beast is slain by the hero Theseus. All of these visions were exemplified in the performance. I took the opportunity to look at the musical score. It was terrifying to say in the least. The performance was heroic – to say the least. To conclude the program the ensemble performed Claude Debussy’s evocative String Quartet. If the performance had been recorded, it could be aired on any radio station with success. I, for one, would have preferred a more French interpretation. It was the case of a wonderful musical group playing a wonderful French composition. The only thing missing was the evocation of the muse of Debussy. In culinary terms, a comparison might be made by serving Beef Stroganoff and calling it, with a French accent, boeuf aux sauce St-rue gran Oeuf and served on Sevres porcelain. The concept of playing in a variety of national styles is often relegated to the history books. What we heard on Sunday was an entirely modern concept…and spectacularly so.

All seemed calm on the surface in advance of Berkeley Symphony musicians’ opening chamber music concert of the 2021-22 season. And then I was informed of some heroic performances. A couple of the performers who were originally announced to play the concert had to cancel due to schedule conflicts. In ordinary times that might spell disaster, and usually the concert might be canceled. But it wasn’t. The substitute players played heroically. Winter from Antonio Vivaldi‘s ubiquitous Four Seasons served as a perfect warm up. His bow skipped along the string like a smooth stone skittering across the surface of a lake. That’s called a flying staccato. Not only that but Nabors’ composition calls for bowed notes to be combined with Pizzicato notes played simultaneously. Paganini invented this technique, but composer Brian Nabors gave it a 21st century touch. If it was difficult and virtuosic. What made it all the more interesting was that it was played with consummate ease. Immediately after the solo piece, Armstrong was joined by violinist Emanuella Nikiforova, violist Ivo Bokulic, and cellist Isaac Pastor-Chermak. They wowed the audience with a new piece, Jessie Montgomery’s string quartet entitled Voodoo Dolls. This was really scary stuff. It reminded me of the mythical labyrinth of Knossos. To conclude the program the ensemble performed Claude Debussy’s evocative String Quartet. If the performance had been recorded, it could be aired on any radio station with success. I, for one, would have preferred a more French interpretation. It was the case of a wonderful musical group playing a wonderful French composition. The only thing missing was the evocation of the muse of Debussy. In culinary terms, a comparison might be made by serving Beef Stroganoff and calling it, with a French accent, boeuf aux sauce St-rue gran Oeuf and served on Sevres porcelain. The In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform at Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday, December 19, showcasing the Center’s Steinway Grand Piano. The Trio consists of pianist Bill Jackman, bass player Rich Trevor, and drummer Anthony Pegram, who perform as an old-school, classic jazz piano trio. The concert, entitled Music for the Holidays, will be a benefit for the Center and will include a collection of jazz, Latin, swing, and ballads. Jackman has been with the trio for the past 27 years. He was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher and has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Bassist Trevor grew up in Chicago and draws influence from blues and R&B, eventually becoming the bassist for Eli’s Mile High Club in Oakland. Pegram has been a drummer for jazz combos and big bands in the Bay Area for over 40 years. Most recently, he accompanied singer Marcella Hooks and pianist Rodney Burge as the house trio for the Sunday Jazz Brunch at Scott’s Restaurant in Jack London Square. The concert will be performed at 2 p.m. Tickets are $20 at the door, or may be purchased in advance at https://bpt. me/5316993. Proof of vaccination and masking indoors is required.

articles.text: Over the many years that I’ve been writing this column, I feel consistently called to consider the theme of slow, conscious living: slowing down, savoring, and weaving the stories of artisans and the lives of the makers into the products we consume. I think these values are a carry-forward from the many years I spent in the restaurant business watching chefs thoughtfully select the produce, the vendors, and even the place settings for their restaurants. My mission of creating beauty as a spiritual practice evolved over time. It wasn’t always there. In fact, the truth is quite the opposite. In my youth I had the gift of contrast. I worked in a wide range of food industry establishments, starting with McDonalds at age 16, the Sizzler at 17, and working my way up through the ranks of various restaurants until I wound up 15 years later as a seasoned restaurant professional working in the highest-end establishments San Francisco had to offer. During that time, I frequented many restaurants as a “professional” foodie and enjoyed hundreds of meals prepared by many of our wonderful Bay Area chefs. I also traveled, touring (and eating my way) through France and Italy. I even had one lucky week of getting to cook with Jean Pierre Moule, a founding chef with Alice Waters at Chez Panisse. I watched. I learned. I developed a strong understanding that the food that satisfied all the senses — not just my palate, but my heart and soul – was food that had been prepared slowly, thoughtfully, and served in an environment where beauty and simplicity were strongly revered. The most memorable of my experiences as a restaurant professional were the years I spent on the sidelines of Alice Waters’ incubator-by-proxy when I was in a five-year relationship with a waiter at Chez Panisse. articles.text: Tips for year-end and beyond from your local Scout Council As you may recall, with the Federal Tax Law that was signed into law on December 22, 2017, most taxpayers have or will claim the Standard Deduction and have lost the benefit of Itemized Deductions. Charitable contributions are still deductible, but in many cases, with the limitations of deductible taxes and mortgage interest, coupled with the elimination of miscellaneous deductions, many will fall below the Standard Deduction amount. Keep in mind that California did not conform to the Federal Tax Law changes. Here are some strategies for you to consider: ● For those who are subject to the RMD (required minimum distribution) rules for your retirement accounts, you are eligible to do a QCD (qualified charitable distribution). With a QCD you can distribute up to $100,000 of your annual RMD to the church or other qualified 501(c)(3) public charity, enabling you to avoid paying income taxes on that amount. ○ When you reach age 70-1/2 you are subject to the RMD rules. However, changes were made with the SECURE Act, signed into law on December 10, 2019, whereby if your 70th birthday is on or after July 1, 2019, you do not have to take withdrawals until you reach age 72. ○ If you are subject to the RMD rules and do not take the required distribution, you are subject to a 50% tax penalty on the undistributed amount. ○ With the CARES Act, the IRS suspended the required distributions only for the tax year 2020. ○ For the tax year 2021 and beyond, the required distributions again apply. ● Consider bunching up multiyear charitable contributions into one year, along with your other eligible deductions, to exceed the Standard Deduction amount. These are strategies to be discussed with your personal tax advisor. John Chiang is a CPA and a member of the Piedmont Council BSA Finance Committee.

Piedmont Seniors purchased new, unwrapped toys for children of all ages to be put in the toy donation bins at the Fire Station. Many lower income children and their parents have come to depend on this important program to ensure that their children have a joyful Christmas. The Fire Department welcomes more donations during this holiday season. • Socks for Seniors Piedmont Seniors has supported Socks for Seniors for 9 years. One of the local nursing homes lost 1/3 of its population this year. The Lutheran Ministry serves four local nursing homes: Crown Bay in Alameda and Oakland, Fruitvale Convalescent, Willow Tree, and Bay Area Health Care. Pictured are: Albert Chen, Phil Witte, Karin Fetherston, Ken Young, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Laura Goldman, Melba Yee, Mike and Nancy Henn, Lois Price, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Fourteen members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group gathered in front of the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park on a cool afternoon on Monday, December 6, for a discussion of their December book, Michael Lewis’ non-fiction The Premonition: A Pandemic Story. Carol and Swee Ling brought Santa-worthy sacks of refreshments that the readers barely made a dent in. The dictionary defines “premonition” as “a strong feeling that something is about to happen, especially something unpleasant.” If the group had a premonition last Monday, it might have been about the weather. The temperature dipped to 52 by the time the group finished its discussion prior to 3 p.m. Michael Lewis is a great storyteller. On the back cover of The Premonition, John Williams of the New York Times Book Review writes, “I would read an 800-page history of the stapler, if he (Lewis) wrote it.” Members of the group who had read previous works by Lewis, such as Moneyball, The Big Short, The Blind Side, and Liar’s Poker, would agree with Williams. The group felt it is an important and thought-provoking book, but also one that raises concerns about our country. Lewis tells the story of how the pandemic came to be, but also how it was able to spread so quickly in the United States. He writes that the American coronavirus pandemic was a perfect storm of the reaction of President Trump, the long history of politicization of the Center for Disease Control (CDC) and the lack of a unified public health care system – all coming together with horrible consequences. This is also the story of a random group of experts whose jobs it was to put together plans for responding to pandemics in general. When the Covid-19 virus struck our country and our government’s response was sorely lacking, these public health officers, doctors, and researchers took the initiative to try to save Americans from the Covid-19 disaster. Charity Dean, a public health doctor in California, saw the danger of the virus before the rest of the country did. She tried unceasingly to get state officials to look at the data and act to keep the virus from spreading. In doing so, she put her reputation and her job in jeopardy. There also was another group of doctors trying to do the same thing at the federal level. This book is a particular indictment of the CDC. Years ago, a CDC official took steps to avoid a potential pandemic that turned out not to be serious, but his career was ruined because of his action. It is no wonder that very few leaders of government agencies are willing to take proactive, let along heroic actions in times of trouble. The changes in leadership can also contribute to ineffectiveness. Additionally, government positions that were once reserved for career public servants have been politicized. According to Lewis these political appointees may not have the competence or appropriate motivations to do what is needed, and right for our country. Some members of the reading group were initially concerned that a book about government public health activities would not be interesting. It was just the opposite. The readers found The Premonition to be very readable and entertaining. They enjoyed the profiles of the “good and heroic” people, as well as the “bad” people who did not live up to what the country needed during the pandemic. The failure of our government to act quickly and meet the pandemic’s challenge was frustrating and disappointing. Our health system does not work as well as it should, and our political system seems broken. The inability of our government to take action in this health crisis was also troubling for the readers. After more than an hour of discussion outdoors, the readers were feeling the December temperature and agreed it was time to select future books and adjourn. They had previously selected the novel Hamnet by Maggie O’Farrell for January and The Boys in the Boat by Daniel James Brown for February. The group also selected The Midnight Library by Matt Haig for their March read. The group’s next discussion will be on Monday, January 3, and start at 1:30 p.m. Weather permitting the group will meet in person at the Tea House. If the forecast is for cold or rain, the group will have their discussion via a Zoom call. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Please contact the Piedmont Recreation Department at 420-3070 for more information. articles.text: Susan Simon Crown, 57, of Piedmont died Monday morning, November 22, 2021, after a twenty-month battle with pancreatic cancer. Susan died at home, surrounded by her husband Greg, her children Katherine and George, and family as she had wished. Throughout her cancer journey, she continued to live a full, connected life with the things she cared about as a priority, and surrounded by the people she loved. Her family, sisters, and nieces and nephews were a tremendous comfort and support for her. She found time to share with others who were on the same journey, offering encouragement and the benefit of what she had learned in her treatment. Susan was remarkable in her ability to be grateful, compassionate, connected, and present despite successes and setbacks and the unpleasantness that she had to endure. Born in Poughkeepsie, NY, she was the daughter of Joseph and Mary Louise Crown, the third of four sisters. She attended the local high school where she rowed crew on the Hudson River, earned her bachelor’s degree in English and Design at Hartwick College in Oneonta, NY, and then landed a job in Boston at Bain & Company. She moved into marketing in the nascent computer publishing industry with a stint at PC Computing, and then relocated to San Francisco to work at Berkeley Systems. In the late 1990s, she joined an early startup to lead their marketing effort. Like many of the dot com era the startup didn’t work out, but she did meet her future husband Greg at the company. Susan and Greg were married in October of 2001 in the Hudson Valley among fall colors – Susan’s favorite time of year. After the birth George, her 2nd child, the couple relocated from San Francisco to Piedmont. As her children reached their teens, Susan channeled some of her energy into a new career with J. Hilburn as a men’s clothing Susan Crown stylist. As with many of Susan’s personal connections, her clients frequently became friends. Susan was never happier than when she was combing a beach intent on finding that special heart-shaped rock or bit of “rare” blue sea-glass. Whether on Rodeo Beach in Marin County, or a beach on Cape Cod, MA or Little Compton, RI, Susan could find the most amazing heart rocks and collectible bits. She avidly collected and curated them and could always tell you where she found each one. More than once TSA questioned the weight and contents of her carry-on bag as she returned from an East Coast trip loaded with precious finds. Susan had a passion for children’s issues and tirelessly supported the San Francisco Court Appointed Special Advocates (SFCASA), organization. She served on the board for many years, drove incredible fundraising (for which she was honored), and spent countless hours personally volunteering. She had a tremendous knack for turning “passion into action” to improve the experiences of youth and families trying to navigate the foster care system. In addition to family and friends, hearts, and CASA, Susan’s other great love was art. She was a strong supporter of art education through local nonprofit work. She had a lifelong personal interest in painting which she renewed and deepened in recent years. Art classes with her sisters Mary and Jane, and frequent small works in watercolor and acrylic created wherever she had a quiet moment gave her both peace and satisfaction. She was nurturing and kind, creative, tenacious, and a fighter for the people and things she loved. Susan had bottomless energy and passion for her family, her friends, and for her causes. She was energized by people she met and with whom she connected. She could make a new friend for life in the space of an airplane ride. Her family and community have lost her, but we are so grateful that she shared herself and her love with us and thereby made us rich. Susan is survived by her husband Greg, children Katherine and George, sister and brother-in-law, Mary and William in MA, sister Jane in NC, beloved nieces and nephews in MA and universities in Washington DC and VA, and dear friends all across the country. A celebration of Susan’s life will be held at the Episcopal Church of St. Mary the Virgin on Union Street in San Francisco at 10 a.m. on Wednesday, January 5th. In lieu of flowers, please make contributions in Susan’s memory to the pancreatic cancer support organization “Let’s Win” (https://letswinpc.org) or the “Pancreatic Cancer Action Network” (https://www.pancan.org). articles.text: Madeleine Hickling, a longtime Piedmont resident, passed away on December 2, 2021. Madeleine Henning Hickling died on December 2, 2021 from complications of kidney disease that first became apparent after a bout of liposarcoma in the 2000s. A native of St. Cloud, Minnesota, Maddy lived in the Bay Area since 1960, when she met and married her husband, Douglas Hickling. Maddy had many interests in the community and over the years participated in several organizations including the University YWCA Auxiliary, Town and Gown Club, the Bellevue Club, and the Piedmont Area Republican Women. Maddy took pride in being a native Minnesotan and a graduate of the U of Minnesota, where she studied psychology and joined Kappa Kappa Gamma Sorority. Maddy remained involved in the KKG alumni association for decades and valued the friendships she made as an alumna. Until recently Maddy kept up with several childhood friends from St. Cloud who, like her, graduated from the St. Cloud State Laboratory High School and later relocated to California. Until the final days of her life, Maddy was highly engaged with the world around her and keenly appreciated things that brought beauty and comfort to everyday life. She was an avid gardener who loved raising flowers and vegetables and herbs. She had a green thumb with houseplants, especially orchids. She participated in the East Bay Earthworms gardening group for many years. She also enjoyed home interior decoration and design, which led her to a career in residential real estate serving Piedmont, first as an agent with Century 21, then later with Mason-McDuffie (which became Better Homes Realty). Seasonal rituals and holidays were important to her, and she established fun family traditions like eating special meals in the dining room on holidays Halloween and Valentine’s Day and hosting family Christmas and Easter celebrations. Maddy is survived by her children, Anne Hickling of Phoenix, Arizona, and William Hickling of Alameda. She is also survived by her sister, Emily Henning Warden of Berkeley, and two grandchildren, Luke and Julian Rodriguez, of Phoenix. She is predeceased by her husband, Douglas Hickling, who died in 2014. A memorial celebrating the life of Maddy Hickling will be held on Friday, January 7, 2022 at 10:00 a.m. in the Julia Morgan Chapel at Chapel of the Chimes on Piedmont Avenue. In lieu of flowers and gifts, the family requests that donations be made to the Friends of the Morcom Rose Garden, https://friendsofoaklandrose.org/.

Seasonal rituals and holidays were important to her, and she established fun family traditions like eating special meals in the dining room on holidays Halloween and Valentine’s Day and hosting family Christmas and Easter celebrations. Maddy is survived by her children, Anne Hickling of Phoenix, Arizona, and William Hickling of Alameda. She is also survived by her sister, Emily Henning Warden of Berkeley, and two grandchildren, Luke and Julian Rodriguez, of Phoenix. She is predeceased by her husband, Douglas Hickling, who died in 2014. A memorial celebrating the life of Maddy Hickling will be held on Friday, January 7, 2022 at 10:00 a.m. in the Julia Morgan Chapel at Chapel of the Chimes on Piedmont Avenue. In lieu of flowers and gifts, the family requests that donations be made to the Friends of the Morcom Rose Garden, https://friendsofoaklandrose.org/. Susan Crown dies November 22 in Piedmont Susan Simon Crown, 57, of Piedmont died Monday morning, November 22, 2021, after a twenty-month battle with pancreatic cancer. Susan died at home, surrounded by her husband Greg, her children Katherine and George, and family as she had wished. Throughout her cancer journey, she continued to live a full, connected life with the things she cared about as a priority, and surrounded by the people she loved. Her family, sisters, and nieces and nephews were a tremendous comfort and support for her. She found time to share with others who were on the same journey, offering encouragement and the benefit of what she had learned in her treatment. Susan was remarkable in her ability to be grateful, compassionate, connected, and present despite successes and setbacks and the unpleasantness that she had to endure. Born in Poughkeepsie, NY, she was the daughter of Joseph and Mary Louise Crown, the third of four sisters. She attended the local high school where she rowed crew on the Hudson River, earned her bachelor’s degree in English and Design at Hartwick College in Oneonta, NY, and then landed a job in Boston at Bain & Company. She moved into marketing in the nascent computer publishing industry with a stint at PC Computing, and then relocated to San Francisco to work at Berkeley Systems. In the late 1990s, she joined an early startup to lead their marketing effort. Like many of the dot com era the startup didn’t work out, but she did meet her future husband Greg at the company. Susan and Greg were married in October of 2001 in the Hudson Valley among fall colors – Susan’s favorite time of year. After the birth George, her 2nd child, the couple relocated from San Francisco to Piedmont. As her children reached their teens, Susan channeled some of her energy into a new career with J. Hilburn as a men’s clothing Susan Crown stylist. As with many of Susan’s personal connections, her clients frequently became friends. Susan was never happier than when she was combing a beach intent on finding that special heart-shaped rock or bit of “rare” blue sea-glass. Whether on Rodeo Beach in Marin County, or a beach on Cape Cod, MA or Little Compton, RI, Susan could find the most amazing heart rocks and collectible bits. She avidly collected and curated them and could always tell you where she found each one. More than once TSA questioned the weight and contents of her carry-on bag as she returned from an East Coast trip loaded with precious finds. Susan had a passion for children’s issues and tirelessly supported the San Francisco Court Appointed Special Advocates (SFCASA), organization. She served on the board for many years, drove incredible fundraising (for which she was honored), and spent countless hours personally volunteering. She had a tremendous knack for turning “passion into action” to improve the experiences of youth and families trying to navigate the foster care system. In addition to family and friends, hearts, and CASA, Susan’s other great love was art. She was a strong supporter of art education through local nonprofit work. She had a lifelong personal interest in painting which she renewed and deepened in recent years. Art classes with her sisters Mary and Jane, and frequent small works in watercolor and acrylic created wherever she had a quiet moment gave her both peace and satisfaction. She was nurturing and kind, creative, tenacious, and a fighter for the people and things she loved. Susan had bottomless energy and passion for her family, her friends, and for her causes. She was energized by people she met and with whom she connected. She could make a new friend for life in the space of an airplane ride. Her family and community have lost her, but we are so grateful that she shared herself and her love with us and thereby made us rich. Susan is survived by her husband Greg, children Katherine and George, sister and brother-in-law, Mary and William in MA, sister Jane in NC, beloved nieces and nephews in MA and universities in Washington DC and VA, and dear friends all across the country. A celebration of Susan’s life will be held at the Episcopal Church of St. Mary the Virgin on Union Street in San Francisco at 10 a.m. on Wednesday, January 5th. In lieu of flowers, please make contributions in Susan’s memory to the pancreatic cancer support organization “Let’s Win” (https://letswinpc.org) or the “Pancreatic Cancer Action Network” (https://www.pancan.org).
